nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
This is related to following discussion:
https://github.com/orgs/python-poetry/discussions/8531
Poetry Issue:
python-poetry/poetry#8535
PyTorch related Issue:
#152121
Poetry requires all the wheels in one index should have the same requirements using environment markers like:
numpy >=1.17, <1.18 ; python_version == "3.6"
numpy >=1.18, <1.20 ; python_version == "3.7"

However PyTorch publishes wheels to following indexes:
https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130
https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
https://pypi.org/project/torch/
Pypi torch project https://pypi.org/project/torch/ is composed of different wheels from different download.pytorch.org dubfolders:
Stable CUDA Linux x86 wheels
Linux CPU Aarch64 wheels
Windows x86 CPU wheels
MacOS M1 wheels
Hence while its possible to achieve same metadata for all packages inside 1 index
https://download.pytorch.org folder or https://pypi.org/project/torch/.
Having same metadata in both indexes is not achievable without package metadata modifications, which could be source of potential errors.
This proposition is to stop modifying metadata for packages uploaded to pypi and make sure download.pytorch.org wheels contain same metadata starting from version 2.10
Versions
2.10
cc @seemethere @malfet @tinglvv

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
Source: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1zugXJm47oX4LOGfczk1H0xKs9d_Cn-sm#scrollTo=ahfnmPO3gtS3
Repro:
import torch
from torch import Tensor
from torch.distributed.tensor import (
    DTensor,
    DeviceMesh,
    distribute_tensor,
    init_device_mesh,
    Partial,
    Replicate,
    Shard,
)
from torch.distributed.tensor.placement_types import _StridedShard
from torch.distributed._local_tensor import (
    local_tensor_mode,
    LocalTensor,
    LocalTensorMode,
)
import traceback

S = Shard
R = Replicate()
_SS = _StridedShard

def product(it):
    x = 1
    for i in it:
        x *= i
    return x

def arange_nd(*sizes):
    if len(sizes) == 1 and isinstance(sizes[0], (list, tuple)):
        sizes = sizes[0]
    return torch.arange(product(sizes)).view(sizes)

def reconcile(l: Tensor):
    """Asserts that a LocalTensor is the same on all ranks, and returns the single Tensor."""
    if isinstance(l, LocalTensor):
        return l.reconcile()
    return l

def init_local_tensor_mode(world_size):
    from torch.distributed import _local_tensor
    if _local_tensor._LOCAL_TENSOR_MODE:
        for lm in list(reversed(_local_tensor._LOCAL_TENSOR_MODE)):
            lm.__exit__(None, None, None)
    try:
        torch.distributed.destroy_process_group()
    except AssertionError:
        pass
    torch.distributed.init_process_group(
        "fake",
        rank=0,
        world_size=world_size,
    )
    lm = LocalTensorMode(world_size)
    lm.__enter__()
    return world_size

# https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/pull/29381

world_size = init_local_tensor_mode(4)
mesh = init_device_mesh("cpu", (2, 2), mesh_dim_names=("x", "y"))

a = distribute_tensor(arange_nd(8, 4).float(), mesh, [S(0), S(1)]).requires_grad_()
b = distribute_tensor(arange_nd(4, 6).float(), mesh, [R, S(0)]).requires_grad_()
c = distribute_tensor(arange_nd(8, 4).float(), mesh, [S(0), S(1)]).requires_grad_()
d = distribute_tensor(arange_nd(4, 6).float(), mesh, [R, S(0)]).requires_grad_()
e = a @ b
f = c @ d
g = e + f
h = g.redistribute(placements=[S(0), R])  # comms!
i = h.sum()

e.retain_grad()
f.retain_grad()
g.retain_grad()
h.retain_grad()
i.retain_grad()

from torch.utils._debug_mode import DebugMode
with DebugMode(record_realtensor=False) as debug_mode:
    i.backward()
print(debug_mode.debug_string())

"""
print(a.grad.placements)
print(b.grad.placements)
print(c.grad.placements)
print(d.grad.placements)
print(e.grad.placements)
print(f.grad.placements)
print(g.grad.placements)
print(h.grad.placements)
print(i.grad.placements)
"""

This prints:
  aten::ones_like(dt: f32[]| PR, pin_memory=False, memory_format=torch.preserve_format)
  aten::clone(dt: f32[]| RR, memory_format=torch.contiguous_format)
  aten::expand(dt: f32[]| RR, [8, 6])
  aten::clone(dt: f32[8, 6]| RR, memory_format=torch.contiguous_format)
    redistribute_input(t: f32[8, 6], trace: RR->S(0)R->S(0)P)
  aten::clone(dt: f32[8, 6]| S(0)R, memory_format=torch.contiguous_format)
  aten::clone(dt: f32[8, 6]| S(0)R, memory_format=torch.contiguous_format)
  aten::t(dt: f32[8, 4]| S(0)S(1))
  aten::mm(dt: f32[4, 8]| S(1)S(0), dt: f32[8, 6]| S(0)R)
  aten::t(dt: f32[4, 6]| RS(0))
  aten::mm(dt: f32[8, 6]| S(0)R, dt: f32[6, 4]| RS(1))
  aten::detach(dt: f32[8, 4]| S(0)S(1))
  aten::detach(dt: f32[4, 6]| PS(0))
  aten::clone(dt: f32[8, 6]| S(0)R, memory_format=torch.contiguous_format)
  aten::t(dt: f32[8, 4]| S(0)S(1))
  aten::mm(dt: f32[4, 8]| S(1)S(0), dt: f32[8, 6]| S(0)R)
  aten::t(dt: f32[4, 6]| RS(0))
  aten::mm(dt: f32[8, 6]| S(0)R, dt: f32[6, 4]| RS(1))
  aten::detach(dt: f32[8, 4]| S(0)S(1))
  aten::detach(dt: f32[4, 6]| PS(0))

In particular, look at the redistribute:
    redistribute_input(t: f32[8, 6], trace: RR->S(0)R->S(0)P)

It claims that the tensor is redistributed to partial. But it is not, in DTensor, we have hard-coded that you should stay replicate when this happens.
        output = redistribute_local_tensor(
            local_tensor,
            current_spec,
            previous_spec,
            async_op=async_op,
            is_backward=True,
        )

        if output.dtype != ctx.original_dtype:
            output = output.to(ctx.original_dtype)

        # normalize the target placement to replicate if it is partial
        normalized_placements: list[Placement] = []
        for previous_placement in previous_spec.placements:
            if previous_placement.is_partial():
                # keep target placement to replicate instead of partial in this case
                normalized_placements.append(Replicate())
            else:
                normalized_placements.append(previous_placement)


But because the redistribute hook is in redistribute_local_tensor it reports the P placement (prior to it getting normalized).
The "right" fix is to stop hacking this up with the normalization after the fact, and ask for the redistribute we actually want.
cc @H-Huang @awgu @wanchaol @fegin @fduwjj @wz337 @wconstab @d4l3k @pragupta @msaroufim @dcci @zpcore
Versions
main

Deprecation warning spam about internal behaviour that the user cannot do anything about (see example below).
Minimal example:
import torch

def cli_main():
    torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("high")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    cli_main()

Old settings, e.g, torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True, torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = True, allowTF32CuDNN() and allowTF32CuBLAS() will be deprecated after Pytorch 2.9. nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
Problem Description
When using torch.compile on models that perform FFT operations followed by torch.complex() tensor reconstruction, compilation fails with stride validation errors. The error occurs specifically when reconstructing complex tensors from separately processed real and imaginary parts after FFT operations. The issue is due to inconsistency between fake (meta) kernel stride calculations and actual execution strides.
code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.fft
class SpectralNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_channels=3, num_classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.input_channels = input_channels
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(input_channels, 16, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(16, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.freq_conv = nn.Conv2d(32, 32, kernel_size=1)
        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(
            nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((4, 4)),
            nn.Flatten(),
            nn.Linear(32 * 4 * 4, 128),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(128, num_classes)
        )
    def forward(self, x):
        x = torch.relu(self.conv1(x))
        x = torch.relu(self.conv2(x))
        x_fft = torch.fft.fft2(x)
        x_fft_real = x_fft.real
        x_fft_imag = x_fft.imag
        x_real_processed = self.freq_conv(x_fft_real)
        x_imag_processed = self.freq_conv(x_fft_imag)
        x_processed = torch.complex(x_real_processed, x_imag_processed)
        x_spatial = torch.fft.ifft2(x_processed).real
        output = self.classifier(x_spatial)
        return output
def get_default_model():
    model = SpectralNet(input_channels=3, num_classes=10)
    return model
def get_sample_inputs():
    batch_size = 4
    channels = 3
    height = 32
    width = 32
    x = torch.randn(batch_size, channels, height, width)
    return (x,)
def main():
    model = get_default_model()
    model.eval()
    inputs = get_sample_inputs()
    with torch.no_grad():
        output = model(*inputs)
    print("SpectralNet executed successfully!")
    print(f"Input shape: {inputs[0].shape}")
    print(f"Output shape: {output.shape}")
    print(f"Output strides: {output.stride()}")
    x = torch.randn(8, 16, 32, 32)
    custom_strided = x.as_strided(size=(8, 16, 16, 16),
                                 stride=(16*32*32, 32*32, 32*2, 2))
    print(f"Original tensor strides: {x.stride()}")
    print(f"Custom strided tensor strides: {custom_strided.stride()}")
    x_fft = torch.fft.fft2(x)
    print(f"FFT output strides: {x_fft.stride()}")
    print(f"FFT real part strides: {x_fft.real.stride()}")
    try:
        compiled_model = torch.compile(model)
        with torch.no_grad():
            output_compile = compiled_model(*inputs)

        print(f'Compile  shape: {output_compile.shape}')
    except Exception as e:
        print(f'\nOriginal exception:\n {e}')

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

🐛 Describe the bug
Problem Description:
When using torch.compile with models that contain custom Tensor subclasses, compilation fails during the forward pass when accessing layer weight data to create custom tensor instances. The error occurs specifically when trying to convert regular tensor data (from self.layer1.weight.data) to a custom tensor subclass within the compiled forward method.
code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
class CustomTensor(torch.Tensor):
    def __init__(self, data):
        super().__init__()
        self.custom_metadata = "custom_tensor_data"
    @classmethod
    def __torch_function__(cls, func, types, args=(), kwargs=None):
        if kwargs is None:
            kwargs = {}
        return super().__torch_function__(func, types, args, kwargs)
    def custom_method(self):
        return f"Custom tensor with metadata: {self.custom_metadata}"
class EnhancedCustomTensor(CustomTensor):
    def __init__(self, data):
        super().__init__(data)
        self.enhanced_flag = True
    def enhanced_operation(self):
        return self * 2.0 if self.enhanced_flag else self
class NeuralNetWithCustomTensors(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size=784, hidden_size=128, num_classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.input_size = input_size
        self.layer1 = nn.Linear(input_size, hidden_size)
        self.layer2 = nn.Linear(hidden_size, hidden_size)
        self.output_layer = nn.Linear(hidden_size, num_classes)
        self.activation = nn.ReLU()
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(0.2)
        self.custom_weights = None
        self.enhanced_features = None
    def forward(self, x):
        if not isinstance(x, CustomTensor):
            x = CustomTensor(x)
        self.custom_weights = CustomTensor(self.layer1.weight.data)
        x = self.layer1(x)
        x = self.activation(x)
        x = self.dropout(x)
        intermediate_result = CustomTensor(x)
        self.enhanced_features = EnhancedCustomTensor(intermediate_result)
        x = self.layer2(x)
        x = self.activation(x)
        if self.enhanced_features is not None:
            enhanced_result = self.enhanced_features.enhanced_operation()
            x = x + enhanced_result[:x.size(0), :x.size(1)]
        x = self.output_layer(x)
        return x
    def get_custom_metadata(self):
        if self.custom_weights is not None:
            return self.custom_weights.custom_method()
        return "No custom weights initialized"
def get_default_model():
    model = NeuralNetWithCustomTensors(input_size=784, hidden_size=128, num_classes=10)
    return model
def get_sample_inputs():
    batch_size = 4
    input_size = 784
    x = torch.randn(batch_size, input_size)
    return (x,)
def main():
    model = get_default_model()
    model.eval()
    inputs = get_sample_inputs()
    print("Model architecture:")
    print(model)
    print(f"\nCustom tensor subclass hierarchy: {model.get_custom_metadata()}")
    with torch.no_grad():
        output = model(*inputs)
    print("\nModel executed successfully!")
    print(f"Input shape: {inputs[0].shape}")
    print(f"Output shape: {output.shape}")
    print(f"Output type: {type(output)}")
    print(f"Model parameters: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())}")
    if model.enhanced_features is not None:
        print(f"\nEnhanced features type: {type(model.enhanced_features)}")
        print(f"Enhanced features metadata: {model.enhanced_features.custom_metadata}")
        print(f"Enhanced operation result shape: {model.enhanced_features.enhanced_operation().shape}")

    try:
        compiled_model = torch.compile(model)
        with torch.no_grad():
            output_compile = compiled_model(*inputs)
        print(f'Compile  shape: {output_compile.shape}')
    except Exception as e:
        print(f'\nOriginal exception:\n {e}')
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
Description:
When using torch.compile() inside a CUDA Graph capture context, the compilation process fails because it attempts to access CUDA RNG state, which is prohibited during graph capture. This prevents users from combining two important PyTorch performance optimization features.
code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class TestModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(10, 20)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(20, 1)
        self.relu = nn.ReLU()

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.fc1(x)
        x = self.relu(x)
        x = self.fc2(x)
        return x

def get_default_model():
    return TestModel()

def get_sample_inputs():
    device = torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')
    x = torch.randn(4, 10, requires_grad=True, device=device)
    return (x,)

def main():
    model = get_default_model()
    inputs = get_sample_inputs()
    device = inputs[0].device
    model.to(device)
    model.eval()

    with torch.no_grad():
        original_output = model(*inputs)
        print('Original model output shape:', original_output.shape)

        if torch.cuda.is_available():
            graph = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()
            with torch.cuda.graph(graph):
                compiled_model = torch.compile(model)
                captured_output = compiled_model(*inputs)
            graph_output = graph.run()
            print('Captured graph output shape:', graph_output.shape)
            assert torch.allclose(original_output, graph_output), "Output mismatch between original and graph execution"
        else:
            print("CUDA not available, skipping graph capture")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

🐛 Describe the bug
Description:
This error occurs when using torch.compile() on a model that involves FFT operations with a custom-defined fft_dim. Specifically, the model executes an FFT operation on an input tensor with the specified dimension, but during compilation, the operation fails due to an incorrect stride mismatch. The error message indicates:
code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class FFTModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, fft_dim=0):
        super().__init__()
        self.fft_dim = fft_dim

    def forward(self, x):
        return torch.fft.fft(x, dim=self.fft_dim)

def get_default_model():
    return FFTModel(fft_dim=0)

def get_sample_inputs():
    x = torch.randn(3, 5, 7, requires_grad=True)
    return (x,)

def main():
    model = get_default_model()
    model.eval()
    inputs = get_sample_inputs()
    with torch.no_grad():
        output = model(*inputs)

    print('Output shape:', output.shape)

            output_compile = compiled_model(*inputs)

        print(f'Compile  shape: {output_compile.shape}')

nodes.title: TorchDynamo Compilation Error: Invalid Stride Handling for FFT in Custom Model During Compilation

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
Description：
When compiling a model containing custom Tensor subclasses using torch.compile, a type conversion error occurred.
A MySensor subclass was defined in the code, and methods such as sum, mean, and prod were rewritten. In the forward propagation of the model, transform a regular Tensor into this subclass and perform the corresponding operations. Although the model runs normally in normal mode, when using torch.compile, the internal type system cannot correctly handle custom Tensor subclasses, resulting in type conversion errors. Specifically, during backpropagation, the compiled model fails to correctly convert MySensor subclasses back to standard Tensor types, resulting in errors.
code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class MyTensor(torch.Tensor):
    def sum(self, dim=None, keepdim=False):
        return super().sum(dim=dim, keepdim=keepdim).as_subclass(MyTensor)
    
    def mean(self, dim=None, keepdim=False):
        return super().mean(dim=dim, keepdim=keepdim).as_subclass(MyTensor)
    
    def prod(self, dim=None, keepdim=False):
        return super().prod(dim=dim, keepdim=keepdim).as_subclass(MyTensor)

class TestModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc = nn.Linear(10, 5)
    
    def forward(self, x):
        out = self.fc(x)
        out_subclass = out.as_subclass(MyTensor)
        reduced = out_subclass.sum(dim=1)
        return reduced

def get_default_model():
    return TestModel()

def get_sample_inputs():
    x = torch.randn(4, 10, requires_grad=True)
    return (x,)

def main():
    model = get_default_model()
    inputs = get_sample_inputs()
    x = inputs[0]
    output = model(x)
    target = torch.zeros_like(output)
    loss = F.mse_loss(output, target)
    loss.backward()
    print('TestModel executed successfully!')
    print('Input shape:', x.shape)
    print('Output shape:', output.shape)
    print('Model parameters count:', sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()))
    print('Input gradients shape:', x.grad.shape)
    try:
        compiled_model = torch.compile(model)
        with torch.no_grad():
            output_compile = compiled_model(*inputs)

        print(f'Compile  shape: {output_compile.shape}')
    except Exception as e:
        print(f'\nOriginal exception:\n {e}')

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

import contextlib

import torch

import torch.nn as nn

logging.basicConfig(
    format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s: %(message)s",
    level=logging.INFO,
)


def log_current_memory() -> None:
    total = torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0).total_memory
    allocated = torch.cuda.memory_allocated(0)
    reserved = torch.cuda.memory_reserved(0)
    msg = "Current CUDA memory usage:"

    d = in_dim
    for _ in range(depth):

        d = hidden
    layers += [nn.Linear(d, out_dim)]
    return nn.Sequential(*layers)

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
Description
﻿
torch.compile() fails to compile a simple model using Tensor.copy_() with an integer argument, even though the same model executes successfully in eager mode.
﻿
This inconsistency suggests that TorchInductor’s type validation is stricter than eager semantics, and lacks graceful fallback for non-Tensor arguments.
Such inconsistencies reduce compiler robustness and user trust in torch.compile.
code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class TestModel(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc = nn.Linear(10, 5)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.fc(x)
        src = torch.randn_like(x)
        x.copy_(1)
        return x

def get_default_model():
    return TestModel()

def get_sample_inputs():
    x = torch.randn(3, 10, requires_grad=True)
    return (x,)

def main():
    model = get_default_model()
    model.eval()
    inputs = get_sample_inputs()
    with torch.no_grad():
        output = model(*inputs)
    print('TestModel executed successfully!')
    print('Input shape:', inputs[0].shape)
    print('Output shape:', output.shape)
    print('Model parameters:', sum((p.numel() for p in model.parameters())))
    try:
        compiled_model = torch.compile(model, fullgraph=True)
        with torch.no_grad():
            output_compile = compiled_model(*inputs)

        print(f'Compile  shape: {output_compile.shape}')
    except Exception as e:

if __name__ == '__main__':

nodes.bodyText:
Description
There’s an incorrect code example in the docstring of:
File: torch/onnx/_internal/exporter/_torchlib/ops/nn.py
Location: Around line 123

Current (Broken) Example
attn_weight = torch.softmax(
    (Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) * attn_mask, dim=-1
)
This example has a syntax error and also uses the attention mask incorrectly.

Suggested Fix
The example should follow the correct scaled dot-product attention formula used in PyTorch’s MultiheadAttention.
# Corrected version
scale_factor = 1.0 / math.sqrt(Q.size(-1))
attn_weight = torch.softmax(
    (Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) * scale_factor) + attn_mask, dim=-1
)

Explanation


Adds missing scale factor
The dot product between Q and K should be scaled by 1 / sqrt(d_k) to prevent large values before softmax.


Fixes syntax error
Removes the misplaced comma before dim=-1, ensuring torch.softmax() receives proper arguments.


Corrects mask usage
The mask should be added, not multiplied.
Adding large negative values (e.g., -inf) ensures masked positions have zero probability after softmax.

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Problem
398fdd3 added support for selecting whether a node will fall back to extern kernels on a per-node basis. This was previously supported on a per-target basis via make_fallback, but some use cases require configuring fallbacks based on the properties of an individual FX node, as opposed to the target operation.
Extern fallbacks often come with layout constraints. For example, custom operators may be written to only accept one specific memory layout. This is especially common on non-GPU hardware accelerators.
Layout constraints are configurable per target by modifying this dict. However, that mechanism doesn't support finer-grained decisions like applying different layout constraints to a node based on whether it falls back.
Proposal
Similar to 398fdd3 , we could add metadata that instructs Inductor to apply a specific layout constraint at the node level, as opposed to the operator level.
Alternatives
No response
Additional context

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Currently it requires both arguments to be tensors. So implementing somehting like sqrt(u^2 + x^2), where u is x a tensor requires inefficient allocation of tensors.
Consequently, something like a "soft-plus" in the form $x \to x + \sqrt{a^2 + x^2}$ or normalization to $[-1, 1]$ via $x / \sqrt{a^2 + x^2}$ also become inefficient.
I  hope it's an extremely small change that is easy to do, and can help in some scenarios I described above.
Alternatives

Writing it myself in Triton and implementing the backward pass.
Doing the inefficient way torch.sqrt(u ** 2 + torch.square(x)), or torch.hypot(torch.full_like(u**2, x), x)
Writing the above and using torch.compile, which takes quite a long time to compile the first time the function is invoked.

Additional context
No response

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
PythonArgParser accepts a scalar Tensor in places that expect an IntList. However, the parsing code casts the Tensor to a PyListObject. It just so happens that PyListObject ob_size is the same place as THPVariable's bool isBorrowed_ from MaybeOwned<Tensor> so the parsing code thinks it's an empty list (!?) but none of this makes any sense.
For example, in eager mode:
    x = torch.ones(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
    print(x.sum(dim=torch.tensor(3)))  # Ed, why are we accepting a scalar tensor here?!
    print(x.sum(dim=3))
It also shows up in places where we generate scalar FakeTensors, such as random.randint():
import torch
import random

def foo():
    x = torch.ones(2, 2, 2)
    return x.sum(dim=random.randint(0, 0))  # i.e.,  dim=0

@torch.compile
def foo_compile():
    x = torch.ones(2, 2, 2)
    return x.sum(dim=random.randint(0, 0))  # i.e.,  dim=0

assert foo().shape == foo_compile().shape
cc @albanD @ezyang
Versions
It's on main as of Nov 11, 2025 (fad48ff)

    import torch.distributed._symmetric_memory as torch_symm_mem
    symm_mem_available = True
except ImportError:
    symm_mem_available = False

def run_rendezvous():
    rank = int(os.environ["RANK"])
    world_size = int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"])

    dist.init_process_group(backend="nccl", rank=rank, world_size=world_size)

    if not symm_mem_available:
        print(f"Rank {rank}: Symmetric memory is not available.")
        return

    device = torch.device(f"cuda:{rank}")
    torch.cuda.set_device(device)

    max_size = 1024
    dtype = torch.bfloat16
    buffer = torch_symm_mem.empty(
        max_size // dtype.itemsize,
        device=device,
        dtype=dtype,
    )

    group_name = dist.group.WORLD.group_name
    handle = torch_symm_mem.rendezvous(buffer, group_name)

    tensor_to_reduce = torch.ones(4, device=device, dtype=dtype) * (rank + 1)
    dist.all_reduce(tensor_to_reduce, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM)

    dist.destroy_process_group()
    print(f"Rank {rank}: Script finished successfully.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if "MASTER_ADDR" not in os.environ:
        os.environ["MASTER_ADDR"] = "localhost"
    if "MASTER_PORT" not in os.environ:
        os.environ["MASTER_PORT"] = "29500"
    run_rendezvous()

import torch

🐛 Describe the bug
When there's a 0 in nn.Parameter's shape (e.g. 1x0x16, 0x4x32. Though it seems weird, such parameters are convenient when handling optional params with unfixed shape), the shape of Parameter will incorrectly change when copied to different devices.
A minimal example:
import torch as pt

class ExampleModule(pt.nn.Module): 
    def __init__(self, num_extra_modules: int = 3):
        pt.nn.Module.__init__(self)
        self.base_vec = pt.nn.Parameter(pt.zeros(1, 16))
        self.extra_vec = pt.nn.Parameter(pt.zeros(num_extra_modules, 16))
    
    def forward(self, x: pt.Tensor): 
        print(f"Shape of `self.extra_vec`: {self.extra_vec.shape} on {self.extra_vec.device}")
        return x + pt.concat([self.base_vec, self.extra_vec], dim = 0).sum(0)

model_cpu = ExampleModule(0)
model_parallel = pt.nn.DataParallel(model_cpu, [0, 1])
model_parallel.to(pt.device("cuda:0"))
model_parallel(pt.ones(4, 16).to("cuda:0"))
Expected output:
Shape of `self.extra_vec`: torch.Size([0, 16]) on cuda:0
Shape of `self.extra_vec`: torch.Size([0, 16]) on cuda:1

Actual output:
Shape of `self.extra_vec`: torch.Size([0, 16]) on cuda:0
Shape of `self.extra_vec`: torch.Size([0]) on cuda:1

🐛 Describe the bug
I'm running a kernel, exposed as a Torch custom op, in which some output is copied to a pinned memory tensor on host. The kernel runs and torch.compiles correctly. However, testing it with torch.library.opcheck results in illegal memory accesses.
On inspection, I'm pretty sure that the issue is with the deepcopy that's performed by the opcheck tests; if I run the individual tests from torch.testing._internal with copy_inputs=False, they pass. From printing out pointers, I think the deepcopy is just copying the pinned tensor (which gets a high pointer on my machine, 0x7f...) to a non-pinned CPU tensor (which gets a medium-sized pointer produced by my system memory allocator), which is of course out of bounds for the GPU.
I'm primarily used to writing the kernels and registering them in the Torch library using CUDA C++, so any example necessarily involves a few different files. I put a minimal example up on this GitHub repo.

🐛 Describe the bug
🐛 Describe the bug
The torch.utils.cpp_extension.check_compiler_is_gcc() function only returns True when the compiler basename is exactly 'c++', failing to detect other GCC variants like g++, gcc, g++-13, g++-14, etc.
This affects any PyTorch functionality that relies on GCC detection, causing features to be silently disabled or tests to be incorrectly skipped on systems using versioned GCC compilers.
How to reproduce:
On a system where the default C++ compiler is g++-13 (common on Fedora/RHEL):
from torch.utils.cpp_extension import get_cxx_compiler, check_compiler_is_gcc

compiler = get_cxx_compiler()  # Returns /usr/bin/g++-13
result = check_compiler_is_gcc(compiler)

print(f"Compiler: {compiler}")
print(f"Detected as GCC: {result}")  # False (incorrect!)
Expected result: Detected as GCC: True
Actual result: Detected as GCC: False
Root cause:
In torch/utils/cpp_extension.py, the check_compiler_is_gcc() function only checks if the compiler basename is exactly 'c++':
compiler_path = os.path.realpath(results[0].strip())
if os.path.basename(compiler_path) == 'c++' and 'gcc version' in version_string:
    return True
return False
Impact:

Any feature/test that uses check_compiler_is_gcc() will fail to detect GCC on systems with versioned compilers
GCC-specific optimizations or features may be silently disabled

Environment:

PyTorch version: main/viable/strict
OS: Fedora/RHEL with versioned GCC
Compiler: g++-13, g++-14, or similar

I am working on a PR to fix this issue.

Summary
There is an OS command injection risk in torch/utils/cpp_extension.py in the precompiled-header build helper. The helper constructs a compiler command including user-supplied values (e.g., extra_cflags, extra_include_paths) and executes the command via subprocess.check_output(..., shell=True). If untrusted input reaches those parameters (for example, a service calling load_inline(..., extra_cflags=..., use_pch=True) with user-provided flags), an attacker can inject shell metacharacters and execute arbitrary commands as the Python process user.
Original Thread : https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/security/advisories/GHSA-gfrj-f355-6v3r#advisory-comment-139444
Affected versions

Introduced in Aug 2023 (commit 5ed6047, PR #106696).
Present in PyTorch releases starting with 2.1 and later main/nightly as of 2025.

Severity

Meta Security and @malfet asked me to file me as general bug. Exact comment from Security Issue

 _ @sumantro93 your example highlights the point I was trying to make: it's not framework's responsibility to sanitize the inputs.

For example, In the sample that you've shared, one is allowed to compile and run any untrusted code, which is a huge security issue on its own, so even if this issue is fixed, one is already allowed to execute arbitrary code on the host by the Flask endpoint developer.

Closing, but please do not hesitate to report it as regular issue or propose a pull request that would sanitize the inputs _

Technical details & PoC

The vulnerable pattern constructs a single command string and calls: subprocess.check_output(cmd_string, shell=True, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT).
Proof-of-concept (local):

# repro_pch_bug.py
import os, subprocess
def build_precompile_header(pch_cmd):
    try:
        subprocess.check_output(pch_cmd, shell=True, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT)
    except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
        print('Error:', e)

payload = "false; echo vulnerable > /tmp/pch_exploit"
build_precompile_header(payload)
print('Exploit file exists?', os.path.exists('/tmp/pch_exploit'))


cc @janeyx99 @malfet

the speed of torch.topk is slower since torch>2.5, here is my test script (Nvidia L20, SM89):

torch: 2.4.1, topk latency: 11.30ms
torch: 2.7.1, topk latency: 17.32ms (-51%)

import time
import torch

if __name__ == "__main__":
    BS, VOCAB, K = 128, 8000000, 1000
    x = torch.randn((BS, VOCAB), device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
    walltime = []
    for _ in range(100):
        s = time.time()
        _ = x.topk(k=K, dim=-1)
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        e = time.time()
        walltime.append(e-s)
    walltime = walltime[10:]
    walltime = sum(walltime) / len(walltime)
    print(f"torch: {torch.__version__}, topk latency: {1000 * walltime}ms")

# torch: 2.4.1+cu126, topk latency: 11.30892170800103ms
# torch: 2.7.1+cu126, topk latency: 17.325512568155922ms

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
It looks like torch.compile hardcodes the number of omp threads in the cache. I can see things like #pragma omp parallel num_threads(8) in the cache. And if different number threads is used the performance is much worse. Is it possible to make it compatible for different number of threads? It's quite useful when running on HPC. Naively it sounds to be something very simple. Hopefully one just need to change #pragma omp parallel num_threads(xxx) to #pragma omp parallel?
Alternatives
No response

import torch
import torch.nn as nn




class CustomBackend:
    """
    Custom compile backend class. Each instance can have different state/config.
    """
    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.name = name
        self.call_count = 0

    def __call__(self, gm: torch.fx.GraphModule, example_inputs):
        """
        Backend must be callable with (gm, example_inputs) signature.

        Args:
            gm: The FX graph module
            example_inputs: Example inputs to the graph

        Returns:
            A compiled callable
        """
        self.call_count += 1
        print(f"[{self.name}] Backend called! (call #{self.call_count})")
        print(f"[{self.name}] Graph: {gm.graph}")
        print(f"[{self.name}] Number of nodes: {len(list(gm.graph.nodes))}")

        # You can modify the graph here if needed
        # For now, just return the graph module which will execute eagerly
        return gm


class MultiplyModule(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

    def forward(self, x, y):
        return x * y


class B(MultiplyModule):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()


# Create two instances
multiply_module_1 = MultiplyModule()
multiply_module_2 = B()

# Create compiled versions
options = {"guard_filter_fn": lambda x: [False for _ in x]}
_compiled_callable1 = torch.compile(
    multiply_module_1.forward,
    fullgraph=True,
    options=options,
    backend=CustomBackend("hi")
)
_compiled_callable2 = torch.compile(
    multiply_module_2.forward,
    fullgraph=True,
    options=options,
    backend=CustomBackend("bi")

)

# Create sample inputs
x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
y = torch.tensor([4.0, 5.0, 6.0])

# Run the compiled callables
result1 = _compiled_callable1(x, y)
result2 = _compiled_callable2(x, y)

print("Result from compiled callable 1:", result1)
print("Result from compiled callable 2:", result2)

import torch
from torch.distributed._tensor import distribute_tensor, Replicate, Shard
from torch.testing._internal.distributed._tensor.common_dtensor import DTensorTestBase

import torch
from torch.library import Library

import torch
from torch.distributed._tensor.experimental import register_sharding
from torch.testing._internal.distributed._tensor.common_dtensor import with_comms
from torch.testing._internal.common_utils import run_tests

foo = Library("foo", "DEF")  # noqa: TOR901
foo.define("my_test_func(Tensor x, Tensor y, Tensor batch_sizes, bool trans_a, bool trans_b, int aicore=-1, * ,Tensor[] out) -> (Tensor, Tensor)")


@torch.library.impl(foo, "my_test_func", "CUDA")
def mlp_gmm_npu(x, y, batch_sizes, trans_a, trans_b, aicore_num=-1, *, out):
    return x.clone(), x.clone()

@torch.library.impl(foo, "my_test_func", "Meta")
def meta_mlp_gmm(x, y, batch_sizes, trans_a, trans_b, aicore_num=-1, *, out):
    return (torch.empty_like(x), torch.empty_like(x))

@register_sharding(torch.ops.foo.my_test_func.default)
def custom_mlp_add(
    x, y, batch_sizes, trans_a=False, trans_b=False, aicore_num=-1, *, out
):
    acceptable_shardings = []
    # add all replicate strategy
    replcate_strategy = (
        [
            Replicate(),
            Replicate(),
        ],
        [
            Replicate(),
            Replicate(),
            Replicate(),
            None,
            None,
            None,
        ]
    )

    acceptable_shardings.append(replcate_strategy)
    return acceptable_shardings

class TestMathOps(DTensorTestBase):
    @with_comms
    def test_mlp_gmm_forward(self):
        device_mesh = self.build_device_mesh()

        a = 2
        b = 1
        c = 1
        bs = torch.Tensor([2620]).to(torch.int32).cuda()
        x = torch.randn(a, b, dtype=torch.bfloat16).cuda()
        w1 = torch.randn(a, b, c, dtype=torch.bfloat16, ).cuda()
        w2 = torch.randn(a, c, b, dtype=torch.bfloat16, ).cuda()
        out1 = torch.randn(a, c, b, dtype=torch.bfloat16, ).cuda()
        out2 = torch.randn(a, c, b + 1, dtype=torch.bfloat16, ).cuda()
        #normal tensor test
        y1 = torch.ops.foo.my_test_func(x, w1, bs, False, False, out=[out1, out2])

        print('=================')
        #distribute tensor
        dist_x = distribute_tensor(x, device_mesh, [Replicate()])
        dist_w1 = distribute_tensor(w1, device_mesh, [Shard(2)])
        dist_w2 = distribute_tensor(w1, device_mesh, [Shard(1)])
        dist_bs = distribute_tensor(bs, device_mesh, [Replicate()])
        dist_out1 = distribute_tensor(out1, device_mesh, [Replicate()])
        dist_out2 = distribute_tensor(out2, device_mesh, [Replicate()])
        dist_y1, dist_y2 = torch.ops.foo.my_test_func(dist_x, dist_w1, dist_bs, False, False, out=[dist_out1, dist_out2])

        print(dist_y2[0].placements)
        print("test torch.ops.foo.my_test_func okokok")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_tests()

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
🐛 Bug Description
PyTorch optimizers (e.g., AdamW, Adam) accept betas parameter as any sequence-like object without type validation. When an OmegaConf ListConfig object is passed, it leads to unexpected behavior during checkpoint serialization because ListConfig retains references to the entire configuration tree.
To Reproduce
import torch
from torch.optim import AdamW
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

# Create a config with nested structure
cfg = OmegaConf.create({
    'model': {'betas': [0.9, 0.999]},
    'data': {'batch_size': 32},
    # ... other configurations
})

# Create optimizer with OmegaConf ListConfig (no error raised)
model = torch.nn.Linear(10, 1)
optimizer = AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, betas=cfg.model.betas)

# Save checkpoint
checkpoint = {
    'optimizer_state_dict': optimizer.state_dict()
}
torch.save(checkpoint, 'checkpoint.pt')

# The entire config tree is serialized due to ListConfig._parent reference!
# This causes:
# 1. Unexpectedly large checkpoint files
# 2. PyTorch 2.6+ loading failures with weights_only=True
Expected behavior
The optimizer should validate that betas is a tuple or list, and raise a TypeError if other sequence-like objects are passed:
if not isinstance(betas, (tuple, list)):
    raise TypeError(f"betas should be a tuple or list, got {type(betas)}")
Alternatively, convert the input to tuple:

Actual behavior
The scripts I check my checkpoint below:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Script to inspect PyTorch checkpoint files and find all OmegaConf ListConfig objects.
"""

import sys
import torch
from pathlib import Path
from omegaconf import ListConfig, DictConfig


def inspect_value(obj, path="root", found_objects=None, visited=None):
    """
    Recursively inspect an object and find all OmegaConf ListConfig instances.
    
    Args:
        obj: Object to inspect
        path: Current path in the object tree
        found_objects: List to store found ListConfig objects
        visited: Set of visited object ids to avoid infinite recursion
    """
    if found_objects is None:
        found_objects = []
    if visited is None:
        visited = set()
    
    # Avoid infinite recursion by checking if we've seen this object
    obj_id = id(obj)
    if obj_id in visited:
        return found_objects
    visited.add(obj_id)
    
    # Check if current object is ListConfig
    if isinstance(obj, ListConfig):
        found_objects.append({
            'path': path,
            'type': 'ListConfig',
            'value': obj,
            'length': len(obj)
        })
        print(f"Found ListConfig at: {path}")
        print(f"  Length: {len(obj)}")
        print(f"  Content: {obj}")
        print()
    
    # Check if current object is DictConfig (also from OmegaConf)
    if isinstance(obj, DictConfig):
        found_objects.append({
            'path': path,
            'type': 'DictConfig',
            'value': obj,
            'keys': list(obj.keys())
        })
        print(f"Found DictConfig at: {path}")
        print(f"  Keys: {list(obj.keys())}")
        print()
    
    # Recursively check dictionaries
    if isinstance(obj, dict):
        for key, value in obj.items():
            new_path = f"{path}['{key}']"
            inspect_value(value, new_path, found_objects, visited)
    
    # Recursively check lists and tuples
    elif isinstance(obj, (list, tuple)):
        for idx, item in enumerate(obj):
            new_path = f"{path}[{idx}]"
            inspect_value(item, new_path, found_objects, visited)
    
    # Check object attributes if it has __dict__
    elif hasattr(obj, '__dict__') and not isinstance(obj, (str, bytes, int, float, bool, type(None))):
        try:
            for key, value in obj.__dict__.items():
                new_path = f"{path}.{key}"
                inspect_value(value, new_path, found_objects, visited)
        except:
            pass
    
    return found_objects


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        print("Usage: python inspect_pt_omegaconf.py <path_to_pt_file>")
        print("Example: python inspect_pt_omegaconf.py checkpoints/step_5000.pt")
        sys.exit(1)
    
    pt_file = Path(sys.argv[1])
    
    if not pt_file.exists():
        print(f"Error: File not found: {pt_file}")
        sys.exit(1)
    
    print(f"Loading checkpoint: {pt_file}")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Load with weights_only=False to allow loading OmegaConf objects
    try:
        checkpoint = torch.load(pt_file, weights_only=False, map_location='cpu')
        print(f"✓ Successfully loaded checkpoint")
        print()
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"✗ Failed to load with weights_only=False: {e}")
        print()
        return
    
    # Inspect the checkpoint
    print("Inspecting checkpoint for OmegaConf objects...")
    print("=" * 80)
    print()
    
    found_objects = inspect_value(checkpoint)
    
    print("=" * 80)
    print(f"Summary: Found {len(found_objects)} OmegaConf objects")
    print()
    
    if found_objects:
        print("All OmegaConf objects found:")
        for idx, obj_info in enumerate(found_objects, 1):
            print(f"{idx}. Path: {obj_info['path']}")
            print(f"   Type: {obj_info['type']}")
            if obj_info['type'] == 'ListConfig':
                print(f"   Length: {obj_info['length']}")
            elif obj_info['type'] == 'DictConfig':
                print(f"   Keys: {obj_info['keys']}")
            print()
    else:
        print("No OmegaConf ListConfig or DictConfig objects found in the checkpoint.")
    
    # Also show top-level keys
    print("=" * 80)
    print("Top-level keys in checkpoint:")
    if isinstance(checkpoint, dict):
        for key in checkpoint.keys():
            value = checkpoint[key]
            value_type = type(value).__name__
            if isinstance(value, dict):
                print(f"  - {key}: dict with {len(value)} keys")
            elif isinstance(value, (list, tuple)):
                print(f"  - {key}: {value_type} with {len(value)} items")
            elif isinstance(value, (ListConfig, DictConfig)):
                print(f"  - {key}: {value_type} ← OmegaConf object!")
            else:
                print(f"  - {key}: {value_type}")


if __name__ == "__main__":

🐛 Describe the bug
Have a look at the following reproduction:
In [1]: import torch

In [2]: x = torch.rand(2, device="cuda")
         
In [3]: a = torch.rand(2, 3, device="cuda")

In [4]: b = torch.rand(3, 2, device="cuda")

In [5]: f = lambda x, a, b: torch.nn.functional.relu(torch.addmm(x, a, b, alpha=0.5, beta=0.5))

In [6]: fc = torch.compile(f)

In [7]: f(x, a, b)
Out[7]: 
tensor([[0.7411, 0.6704],
        [0.5025, 0.4090]], device='cuda:0')

In [8]: fc(x, a, b)
Out[8]: 
tensor([[1.4822, 1.3408],
        [1.0049, 0.8180]], device='cuda:0')
The fx pass replaces addmm with add(mm) because there is a point-wise user (relu). The problem is that the pattern matching ignores parameters alpha/beta and alpha/beta are being silently replaced with value 1.

🐛 Describe the bug
When using bfloat16 autocast and using nn.RMSNorm with a linear layer before it, torch will not dispatch to the fused RMSNorm since input dtype is bfloat16 (from the linear layer I assume) and the dtype of the RMSNorm weight is float32. However, if I am not mistaken, autocast should choose RMSNorm to either run in float32 or bfloat16 and then cast weight/input accordingly such that they match and can be dispatched to the fused implementation, right?
Below is a script to reproduce this, tested on most recent pytorch version:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
class MinimalRMS(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, apply_linear=False, layernorm=nn.RMSNorm):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = nn.Linear(4, 4) if apply_linear else nn.Identity()
        self.apply_linear = apply_linear
        self.layernorm = layernorm(4, elementwise_affine=True)
    
    def forward(self, x):
        if self.apply_linear:
            x = self.linear(x)
        x = self.layernorm(x)
        return x


if __name__ == "__main__":

    input_cfgs = [
        {'apply_linear': False, 'layernorm': nn.RMSNorm},
        {'apply_linear': True, 'layernorm': nn.RMSNorm},
        {'apply_linear': False, 'layernorm': nn.LayerNorm},
        {'apply_linear': True, 'layernorm': nn.LayerNorm},
    ]
    for cfg in input_cfgs:
        print(f"\nTesting MinimalRMS with apply_linear={cfg['apply_linear']}, layernorm={cfg['layernorm'].__name__}")
        model = MinimalRMS(**cfg).to('cuda')
        input_tensor = torch.randn(2, 4, device='cuda')
        with torch.autocast(device_type="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
            output = model(input_tensor)
        print(output.grad_fn)

which produces this output:
Testing MinimalRMS with apply_linear=False, layernorm=RMSNorm
<FusedRmsNormBackward0 object at 0x773e79a3dc00>

Testing MinimalRMS with apply_linear=True, layernorm=RMSNorm
/home/finn/miniconda3/envs/habitat_py310/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/nn/functional.py:2949: UserWarning: Mismatch dtype between input and weight: input dtype = c10::BFloat16, weight dtype = float, Cannot dispatch to fused implementation. (Triggered internally at /pytorch/aten/src/ATen/native/layer_norm.cpp:344.)
  return torch.rms_norm(input, normalized_shape, weight, eps)
<ToCopyBackward0 object at 0x773e79a3fdf0>

Testing MinimalRMS with apply_linear=False, layernorm=LayerNorm
<NativeLayerNormBackward0 object at 0x773e79a3dc00>

Testing MinimalRMS with apply_linear=True, layernorm=LayerNorm
<NativeLayerNormBackward0 object at 0x773e79a3fdf0>

I can also reproduce this on stable release and older versions. Is this expected? If so, is it recommended to instantiate those RMSNorm layers as bfloat16 (which would no longer let autocast control this)?

🐛 Describe the bug
When running torch.fx.passes.fake_tensor_prop.FakeTensorProp on a graph containing aten.polar with dynamic  shapes, the output shapes become concretized to the example input sizes. This is unexpected—symbolic dims should be preserved. This appears to stem from aten.polar’s fake/meta behavior. Reverting the change introduced in #160894
fixes the issue.
Minimal repo:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

from torch.export import export, Dim
from torch.fx import GraphModule
from torch.fx.passes.fake_tensor_prop import FakeTensorProp
from torch._export.utils import _detect_fake_mode_from_gm

class PolarToy(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, head_dim: int = 32):
        super().__init__()
        self.head_dim = head_dim

    def forward(self, x):
        freqs = x.tanh()
        ones_like = torch.ones_like(freqs)
        freqs_cis = torch.polar(ones_like, freqs)
        return freqs_cis.real + freqs_cis.imag


def export_with_2d_dynamic_batch(mod: nn.Module, device: str = "cpu") -> GraphModule:
    mod = mod.to(device).eval()
    sample = torch.randn(2, 3, 32, device=device)
    dynamic_shapes = ({0: Dim("s0", min=1, max=1024), 1: Dim("s1", min=1, max=2048)},)
    ep = export(mod, (sample,), dynamic_shapes=dynamic_shapes, strict=False)
    gm = ep.module() if hasattr(ep, "module") else ep
    if not isinstance(gm, GraphModule):
        raise RuntimeError("Expected a GraphModule from export().")
    return gm


def main():
    device = "cpu"
    hidden = 7
    mod = PolarToy(hidden)
    gm = export_with_2d_dynamic_batch(mod, device=device)
    gm.print_readable()

    inps = [node.meta.get("val") for node in gm.graph.nodes if node.op == "placeholder"]
    fake_mode = _detect_fake_mode_from_gm(gm)
    FakeTensorProp(gm, fake_mode).propagate(*inps)
    gm.print_readable()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()


Observed output
Before FakeTensorProp :
tanh:      "f32[s77, s27, 32]" = aten.tanh.default(x)
ones_like: "f32[s77, s27, 32]" = aten.ones_like.default(tanh, pin_memory = False)
polar:     "c64[s77, s27, 32]" = aten.polar.default(ones_like, tanh)

After FakeTensorProp:
tanh:      "f32[2, 3, 32]" = aten.tanh.default(x)
ones_like: "f32[2, 3, 32]" = aten.ones_like.default(tanh, pin_memory = False)
polar:     "c64[2, 3, 32]" = aten.polar.default(ones_like, tanh)

Notably, the concretization starts at the aten.polar site and then propagates.
Versions
PyTorch: 2.9.0
Python: 3.12
cc @ezyang @EikanWang @jgong5 @wenzhe-nrv

nodes.title: Dynamo Fails to Trace Python Built-in Function print in Compile Mode

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
Report Description:
﻿
When running a model that involves a GRU layer in TorchDynamo's compiled mode, an error occurs stating that the graph break was purposely triggered for RNN, GRU, and LSTM layers. This behavior appears to be intentionally designed by TorchDynamo, preventing these layers from being traced in the compiled graph. As a result, the model cannot be compiled properly when it includes GRU layers.
﻿
Error Message:
﻿
TorchDynamo purposely graph breaks on RNN, GRU, LSTMs
﻿
Expected Behavior:
GRU layers should be supported in TorchDynamo's compiled mode, or at least an alternative approach should be provided to enable tracing of these layers. This issue makes it difficult to fully utilize TorchDynamo with models that include RNN-based layers such as GRU and LSTM.
code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class AdaptiveFilterRNN(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self, input_dim=8, hidden_dim=16, output_dim=2):
        super().__init__()
        self.a_coeffs = torch.tensor([[0.9995, -1.998, 0.9985], [1.0, -1.95, 0.95]], dtype=torch.float32) * (1.0 + -8.479525107936043e-05)
        self.b_coeffs = torch.tensor([[0.1, 0.15, 0.1], [0.05, 0.1, 0.05]], dtype=torch.float32)
        self.gru = nn.GRU(input_dim, hidden_dim, 2, batch_first=True, dropout=0.2)
        self.attention = nn.MultiheadAttention(hidden_dim, 4, dropout=0.1)
        self.fc_out = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, output_dim)
        self.layer_norm = nn.LayerNorm(hidden_dim)

    def apply_filter_bank(self, x):
        (batch_size, seq_len, features) = x.shape
        filtered_outputs = []
        for batch in range(batch_size):
            batch_filtered = []
            for feat in range(features):
                signal = x[batch, :, feat]
                filter_results = []
                for i in range(len(self.a_coeffs)):
                    a = self.a_coeffs[i]
                    b = self.b_coeffs[i]
                    y = torch.zeros_like(signal)
                    for n in range(len(signal)):
                        if n >= 2:
                            y[n] = b[0] * signal[n] + b[1] * signal[n - 1] + b[2] * signal[n - 2] - a[1] * y[n - 1] - a[2] * y[n - 2]
                    filter_results.append(y)
                combined = torch.stack(filter_results).mean(dim=0)
                batch_filtered.append(combined)
            filtered_batch = torch.stack(batch_filtered, dim=1)
            filtered_outputs.append(filtered_batch)
        return torch.stack(filtered_outputs)

    def forward(self, x):
        x_filtered = self.apply_filter_bank(x)
        (gru_out, _) = self.gru(x_filtered)
        gru_out = self.layer_norm(gru_out)
        (attn_out, _) = self.attention(gru_out.transpose(0, 1), gru_out.transpose(0, 1), gru_out.transpose(0, 1))
        attn_out = attn_out.transpose(0, 1)
        output = self.fc_out(attn_out[:, -1, :])
        return F.softmax(output, dim=1)

def get_default_model():
    return AdaptiveFilterRNN(input_dim=8, hidden_dim=16, output_dim=2)

def get_sample_inputs():
    batch_size = 3
    seq_length = 20
    input_dim = 8
    x = torch.randn(batch_size, seq_length, input_dim) * 0.1
    return (x,)
def main():
    model = get_default_model()
    model.eval()
    inputs = get_sample_inputs()

    print('Filter bank coefficients:')
    print('A coefficients (denominator):')
    print(model.a_coeffs)
    print('B coefficients (numerator):')
    print(model.b_coeffs)

    try:
        with torch.no_grad():
            output_eager = model(*inputs)
        print(f'Eager 输出 shape: {output_eager.shape}')
    except Exception as e:
        print(f'Eager 模式报错: {e}')
    try:
        compiled_model = torch.compile(model, fullgraph=True)
        with torch.no_grad():
            output_compile = compiled_model(*inputs)

        print(f'Compile  shape: {output_compile.shape}')
    except Exception as e:

        print(f'\nOriginal exception:\n {e}')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
Report Description:
When using torch._dynamo.mark_dynamic in the compiled mode with TorchDynamo, an error occurs stating that the function is a "forbidden callable" and cannot be traced. This happens when trying to mark a tensor as dynamic, which is intended for handling dynamic shapes in models. The error prevents models that rely on dynamic shape handling from being successfully compiled and executed with TorchDynamo.
code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch._dynamo

class DynamicRNNModel(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self, input_size=64, hidden_size=128, num_layers=2, num_classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.num_layers = num_layers
        self.lstm = nn.LSTM(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, batch_first=True, bidirectional=True)
        self.attention = nn.MultiheadAttention(hidden_size * 2, num_heads=4, batch_first=True)
        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(hidden_size * 2, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(0.3), nn.Linear(64, num_classes))

    def forward(self, x):
        torch._dynamo.mark_dynamic(x, 0)
        torch._dynamo.mark_dynamic(x, 0)
        (batch_size, seq_len, features) = x.size()
        (lstm_out, (hidden, cell)) = self.lstm(x)
        (attn_out, attn_weights) = self.attention(lstm_out, lstm_out, lstm_out)
        pooled = torch.mean(attn_out, dim=1)
        output = self.classifier(pooled)
        return output

def get_default_model():
    model = DynamicRNNModel(input_size=64, hidden_size=128, num_layers=2, num_classes=10)
    return model

def get_sample_inputs():
    batch_size = torch.randint(4, 16, (1,)).item()
    seq_len = torch.randint(20, 50, (1,)).item()
    features = 64
    x = torch.randn(batch_size, seq_len, features)
    return (x,)

def main():
    model = get_default_model()
    model.eval()
    print('Testing DynamicRNNModel with variable input shapes:')
    for i in range(3):
        inputs = get_sample_inputs()
        with torch.no_grad():
            output = model(*inputs)
        print(f'Test {i + 1}:')
        print(f'  Input shape: {inputs[0].shape}')
        print(f'  Output shape: {output.shape}')
        print(f'  Output range: [{output.min().item():.4f}, {output.max().item():.4f}]')
        print()
    try:
        compiled_model = torch.compile(model)
        with torch.no_grad():
            output_compiled = compiled_model(*inputs)
        print('Compiled mode output shape:', output_compiled.shape)
    except Exception as e:
        print('Compiled mode failed:', str(e))

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

🐛 Describe the bug
Description
When compiling a model with torch.compile, TorchDynamo fails to trace the builtin bool() operator when applied to PyTorch tensors, resulting in a compilation error.

code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch._dynamo

torch._dynamo.config.suppress_errors = False
torch._dynamo.config.verbose = True

class BoolTensorModel(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x, mask):
        make_causal = bool((mask == 0).all())
        print(f"[Forward] make_causal={make_causal}")
        return x + 1

def main():
    x = torch.randn(2, 3)
    mask = torch.zeros(2, 3)

    model = BoolTensorModel()

    eager_out = model(x, mask)
    print("Eager mode output shape::\n", eager_out)

    try:
        compiled_model = torch.compile(model, fullgraph=True)
        compile_out = compiled_model(x, mask)
        print("Compiled mode output shape:\n", compile_out)
    except Exception as e:
        print("Compile error:\n", e)

if __name__ == "__main__":

🐛 Describe the bug
Description
When compiling a neural network model containing complex-valued FFT operations using torch.compile, the compilation fails with a tensor stride assertion error.
code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.fft

class SpectralNet(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self, input_channels=3, num_classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.input_channels = input_channels
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(input_channels, 16, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(16, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.freq_conv = nn.Conv2d(32, 32, kernel_size=1)
        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((4, 4)), nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(32 * 4 * 4, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, num_classes))

    def forward(self, x):
        x = torch.relu(self.conv1(x))
        x = torch.relu(self.conv2(x))
        x_fft = torch.fft.fft2(x)
        x_fft_real = x_fft.real
        x_fft_imag = x_fft.imag
        x_real_processed = self.freq_conv(x_fft_real)
        x_imag_processed = self.freq_conv(x_fft_imag)
        x_processed = torch.complex(x_real_processed, x_imag_processed)
        x_spatial = torch.fft.ifft2(x_processed).real
        output = self.classifier(x_spatial)
        return output

def get_default_model():

def get_sample_inputs():

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/autograd.html#default-gradient-layouts
This page suggests that parameters and gradients have the same stride, although it specifically mentions "parameters" and not "activations". I couldn't find any source on activations.
The below code produces activations and gradients with different strides. In my model, this causes the next layer in the backward to fail.
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

B, H, W, C = 20, 2, 2, 128

x = torch.randn(B, H, W, C, requires_grad=True)
linear = nn.Linear(C, C, bias=False)

values = linear(x)
values.retain_grad()

values_view = values.view(B, H * W, C)
values_view.retain_grad()


def log_grad(name):
    def hook(grad):
        print(f"{name} hook - shape: {grad.shape}, stride: {grad.stride()}")
        return grad

    return hook


print("forward strides", values_view.shape, values_view.stride())
values_view.register_hook(log_grad("values_view"))

weights = torch.randn(B, H * W, C)
result = torch.einsum("bhc,bhc->bc", weights, values_view)

result.backward(torch.ones_like(result))

nodes.bodyText:
Currently, torch.linalg.lu_solve does not support MPS inputs.
I investigated what it would take to add it (my notes about it are here), and it looks relatively straightforward. Looking at existing implementations of lu_solve in PyTorch, jax, mlx, and magma, some of the impls just call directly into an LU solve function from LAPACK or a closed source impl (like CuBLAS). But in all other cases, they are implemented very similarly, with a pair of triangular solve function calls. torch.linalg.solve_triangular already supports MPS inputs, though it doesn't support complex dtypes yet. In my notes I wrote a Python impl of non-batched lu_solve using a pair of triangular solves, and I found that when it's given MPS float inputs, it gives the same result as torch.linalg.lu_solve with inputs converted to CPU.
So the required pieces are already in place to add MPS support to lu_solve for real inputs, and I will add it.
cc @kulinseth @malfet @DenisVieriu97 @jhavukainen

🐛 Describe the bug
A gradient mismatch occurs between eager mode and torch.compile when using torch.autograd.functional.vjp. The discrepancy is observed when using torch.float16 and appears to be dependent on the specific input values provided.
While the forward pass of the compiled function produces results that are numerically very close to the eager version, the backward pass (VJP) computes significantly different gradients for the inputs. This suggests a potential issue in how the backward pass is handled for one or more operations within the compiled graph at float16 precision.
To reproduce:
import torch

def robust_power(base: torch.Tensor, exponent: torch.Tensor, threshold: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    threshold1 = threshold
    result_shape = torch.broadcast_shapes(base.shape, exponent.shape)
    broadcasted_base = torch.broadcast_to(base, result_shape)
    broadcasted_exponent = torch.broadcast_to(exponent, result_shape)
    broadcasted_base = torch.abs(broadcasted_base)
    threshold = torch.broadcast_to(threshold.to(base.dtype), result_shape)
    cond = (broadcasted_exponent < 1 - torch.log(threshold) / torch.log(broadcasted_base)) & (broadcasted_base < threshold)
    output = torch.where(cond, 1 / threshold1 * broadcasted_base, broadcasted_base ** torch.where(cond, 1, exponent))
    return output


base = torch.tensor([[ 0.1331787109375,  0.071533203125, -0.154541015625, -0.0008382797241210938,
                       0.062103271484375, -0.072021484375,  0.0265655517578125,  0.0108489990234375,
                       0.0004291534423828125]], dtype=torch.float16)

exponent = torch.tensor([[ 0.1749267578125], [-0.0286102294921875]], dtype=torch.float16)
threshold = torch.tensor(6.103515625e-05, dtype=torch.float16)

out_grad = torch.tensor([
    [ 0.7158203125, -1.736328125,  1.9599609375, -1.8642578125, -1.720703125,
     -0.30810546875,  0.1309814453125, -1.3525390625, -0.429443359375],
    [-0.7373046875,  0.81591796875,  0.10162353515625,  0.062255859375,  0.587890625,
      0.1507568359375,  1.7099609375, -0.276611328125, -0.52978515625]
], dtype=torch.float16)

# ----------------------------
# Eager (uncompiled) execution
# ----------------------------
print("\n=== Eager Execution ===")
y_normal = robust_power(base, exponent, threshold)
print("Output:\n", y_normal)

y_n, grads_normal = torch.autograd.functional.vjp(
    lambda b, e, t: robust_power(b, e, t),
    (base, exponent, threshold),
    v=out_grad
)
grad_b_n, grad_e_n, _ = grads_normal
print("grad_b (normal):", grad_b_n)
print("grad_e (normal):", grad_e_n)


# ----------------------------
# Compiled execution
# ----------------------------
robust_power_compiled = torch.compile(robust_power)

print("\n=== Compiled function ===")
y_compiled = robust_power_compiled(base, exponent, threshold)
print("Output:\n", y_compiled)

y_c, grads_compiled = torch.autograd.functional.vjp(
    lambda b, e, t: robust_power_compiled(b, e, t),
    (base, exponent, threshold),
    v=out_grad
)
grad_b_c, grad_e_c, _ = grads_compiled
print("grad_b (compiled):", grad_b_c)
print("grad_e (compiled):", grad_e_c)


# ----------------------------
# Comparison
# ----------------------------
print("\n=== Comparison ===")
print("Output equal:", torch.allclose(y_normal, y_compiled, atol=1e-3, rtol=1e-3))
print("grad_b equal:", torch.allclose(grad_b_n, grad_b_c, atol=1e-3, rtol=1e-3))
print("grad_e equal:", torch.allclose(grad_e_n, grad_e_c, atol=1e-3, rtol=1e-3))

model = Model()
